A better analogy, keeping internet pricing models and the zero-rating idea in mind:

  • Adam owns Cargo Rail. They charge per pound to move cargo by train, both the sender and the recipient of the package.
  • Adam opens a delivery company called Speedee Delivery. They compete with Brad's company, Quickie Delivery.
  • Adam gives Speedee Delivery free shipping on Cargo Rail, while still charging Quickie per pound to send.
  • Adam also delivers Speedee boxes to their addresses for free, but still charges Quickie addresses per pound to receive.
  • Soon everyone ships by Speedee simply because nobody wants to pay just for receiving packages.
  • Now Adam has a monopoly both on railyards and delivery companies.
  • Since nobody ships by Quickie anyway, Adam ups the charge per pound to something so ridiculous that nobody can afford it.
  • Now it's impossible for anyone to even start a company that might compete with Speedee, as it wouldn't be cost-effective.

And the chilling Orwellian effect of zero rating packages' ability to control information:

  • Charlie discovers this system and decides to tell everyone about it so something can be done to stop Adam's monopoly.
  • Don't forget that Adam, as a private company owner, can choose to refuse service to anyone at any time for any reason.
  • Adam (as Speedee Delivery) refuses to take any of Charlie's packages and recommends him to Quickie instead.
  • Now Charlie has to pay arbitrary fees just to send a package, caused by Adam's broken pricing model.
  • Even if Charlie could afford to ship packages, nobody would accept them because they now expect Speedee's free delivery.
  • Charlie has no way to tell anyone about Adam's monopoly
  • Adam, if accused of silencing Charlie, can shrug and say "that's just the market, I'm a private business and he's a free entity"
